newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-SW Trains compensation seen 1.75 mln stg.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-SW Trains compensation seen 1.75 mln stg.

text.p: South West Trains, the rail franchise owned by UK transport group Stagecoach Holdings Plc, said on Friday its total bill for compensating passengers for cancellations could approach 1.75 million stg.

Brian Cox, chairman and managing director of South West Trains, said this cost included around 1.3 million stg for the cost of free tickets to customers under its public relations excercise to pacify customers who suffered cancellations plus the additional cost of refunds for problems related to Railtrack Plc signal failures.

Cox said in an interview with Reuters he was confident that the group would be able to reinstate services before Easter (Easter Sunday is March 30) -- in time to avoid a threat from industry regulator Opraf of a one million stg fine and the possible loss of SW Train's franchise.
"We should be able to get services running again by Easter," he said, in time to avoid being "given the red card."
Opraf has warned that it could impose its biggest ever fine if Stagecoach fails to run at least 98.5 percent of services scheduled for SW Trains in April and May.

If the comany still failed to deliver and fell below 97.5 percent of minimum services it would face a possible loss of licence -- a move which would be a serious blow to Stagecoach and the government's privatisation plans.
The problems began when SW Trains axed a number of drivers in a cost-cutting venture only to find it did not have enough drivers to staff the timetable.
Since the new shifts were introduced on January 19, Cox said 2,543 trains had been cancelled.

When asked to comment on the commuter misery, he said: "We can't make an omelette without breaking eggs. We launched a new ship (the franchise) into stormier waters than expected. But we have kept our hand on the tiller and we hope to enter calmer waters soon."
Cox said it was necessary to bear in mind that SW Trains was the first franchise to enter the private sector under the government's sell-off plans.
In the first year, after taking over in February 1996, all targets were reached. "We regret what's happened since. Recent events take the gloss off that. It's a great shame," he said.
He added that some of the cancellations were beyond its control - like signalling failures due to Railtrack's problems.

When asked whether any heads would roll for the debacle, Cox answered: "That is a matter for the board. It is examining the whole issue. But there is no point in changing the people involved, I believe, as it is being handled."
